title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text: Automation must never process partially copied data. This RFC, aligned to RFC 002, defines ingestion readiness criteria, compares file-level and batch-level completion signals, and describes the watch-based chain from ingestion detection to automation execution. The focus is on deterministic gating, auditability, and minimal operational burden, with no implementation changes in this phase.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text: Automation must never process partially copied data. This RFC, aligned to RFC 002, defines ingestion readiness criteria, compares file-level and batch-level completion signals, and describes the watch-based chain from ingestion detection to automation execution. The focus is on deterministic gating, auditability, and minimal operational burden, with no implementation changes in this phase.

text:
Ingestion Requirements

Table 1. Core ingestion requirements for automation mode.







Requirement
Rationale
Implication

Avoid partial copies

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
Completion Signals: File vs Batch
Two patterns dominate ingestion completion: per-file sentinels and batch-level manifests. Both can work, but they impose different operational controls. The table below contrasts the approaches and frames a recommended default.

Table 2. Completion signal trade-offs.








Signal Type
Mechanism
Strengths
Risks




File-level sentinel
.done or .ready per file
Fine-grained control; works for rolling arrivals
More files to manage; risk of partial batch processing.


Batch-level manifest
Single manifest for entire batch
Clear batch boundary; simpler audit trail
Delays partial processing; requires manifest generator.


Stability window
Time-based idle check
No additional files required
Sensitive to large file transfers or slow networks.









NoteRecommendation



Adopt per-file completion signals as the default, backed by hash-based deduplication, and allow batch manifests as an optional higher-level gate when upstream systems can provide them. This aligns with rolling ingestion while preventing duplicate processing and preserving deterministic readiness.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
Discussion: Per-File Readiness and Hashing
A per-file readiness marker (e.g., .done or .ready) matches the expected operational flow for rolling ingestion and keeps the automation responsive. To prevent duplicates, the pipeline should compute or reuse existing file hashes and store them in an ingestion ledger keyed by source path, hash, and timestamp. When a file arrives with a previously seen hash, the system can skip processing or route it to a review queue, preserving idempotency without blocking new data. Hashing also enables integrity verification after transfers and provides an audit-ready fingerprint for compliance reporting.
Batch-level manifests still have value for sites that can generate them reliably, but they should be treated as an optional super-signal rather than the sole gating mechanism. In practice, the watcher can require both a per-file sentinel and hash match, while treating a manifest as a shortcut to mark a group as ready when all entries are present.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
Discussion: Provenance Subfolders and Receipts
A provenance-first layout benefits from deterministic subfolders that allow manual review and reproducible ingestion. A practical pattern is to compute a stable hash from the ingest path relative to the workspace plus a minimal metadata payload (e.g., site ID, modality, acquisition date). This avoids reliance on absolute paths while keeping folder names deterministic across replays. The hashed folder becomes the canonical landing zone for copied data, ensuring repeat runs resolve to the same location.
Add a JSON sidecar receipt in each ingestion subfolder (same basename as the folder) containing the source path, hash inputs, hash output, file list, file hashes, timestamps, and validation status. This receipt enables deduplication, supports audit trails, and simplifies manual review without opening large data files. When updates arrive, the receipt should record a new revision entry rather than overwrite prior metadata.
Best-practice patterns observed in similar pipelines include:

Stable hash inputs that ignore absolute machine paths.
Human-readable aliases stored alongside the hash for review.
Immutable receipts with revision history and operator notes.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
Watcher Strategy (watchfiles + notify)
The ingestion watcher should use watchfiles with the Rust notify backend to minimize latency while preserving readiness gating. Events feed a debounce window, then a readiness validator that checks manifest completeness, sentinel presence, and size stability before enqueueing a run. When readiness fails, the dataset moves to quarantine or remains pending.





flowchart TD
  A[File event] --> B[Debounce window]
  B --> C[Readiness validator]
  C -->|Ready| D[Queue automation run]
  C -->|Not ready| E[Pending or quarantine]
  D --> F[Dispatch serve runtime]


 Figure 1. Ingestion readiness flow with watch-based gating.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
End-to-End Automation Chain
The ingestion plan must describe how readiness transitions into automation execution. The chain below captures the expected order without implementation detail.

File events trigger watch-based detection and debounce.
Readiness validation confirms manifest/sentinel completeness and stability.
A run is queued with taskfile/montage mapping and serve runtime selection.
Automation executes via the serve runtime, writing outputs and logs to the workspace.
Run metadata captures readiness checks, config hashes, and any warnings.

Area
Best Practice
Reason




Ingestion folder
Separate staging from ingestion root
Prevent partial processing.


Completion signal
Prefer per-file sentinel + hash
Keeps rolling ingestion responsive.


Update handling

Avoid silent partial updates.


Deduplication

Prevent duplicate processing.


Quarantine

Keeps operators informed and pipeline clean.


Audit logs
Persist readiness decisions
Supports compliance and debugging.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
Appendix A: Consultant Q&A

Table 4. Consultant responses to ingestion planning questions.






Question
Consultant Answer




What tool generates the batch manifest in upstream systems?
Prefer manifests emitted by the acquisition or export system (CSV/JSON with checksums) so ingestion is deterministic and audit‑ready.


Should incremental updates create a new run or amend the original run?
Default to a new run using a stable batch_id; allow amendments only within a short correction window with a full audit trail.


How long should pending items remain before quarantine?
Keep pending for 24–72 hours; quarantine after 7–14 days without resolution (configurable by site).


Should duplicate hashes be skipped automatically or routed for review?
Treat duplicates as idempotent, skip re‑ingest, and log a duplicate event; optionally route for review in compliance modes.


Which metadata fields should be included in the directory hash input?
batch_id, subject_id, session_id, recording_id, site_id, device_id, export_time, timezone, file_count, total_bytes, manifest_checksum, operator.


How long should receipts be retained before archiving?
Retain 2–7 years depending on IRB/clinical policy; keep receipts immutable and archive rather than delete.

title: RFC 007: Ingestion Planning for Automation
text:
Execution Plan (TDD)
The execution plan below follows a test‑first sequence so ingestion logic is validated before operational rollout. Each phase assumes use of the existing test data and workspace to validate behavior in a controlled setting.

Table 5. TDD execution phases for ingestion work.







Phase
TDD Focus
Example Tests




Phase 1: Readiness gates
Manifest/sentinel validation
Missing fields, file count mismatch, size stability enforcement.


Phase 2: Hashing + dedup
Deterministic hashes
Stable hash output, duplicate detection, checksum mismatch detection.


Phase 3: Receipts
Immutable audit trail
Receipt creation, append‑only revisions, retention policy checks.


Phase 4: Watcher chain
Event handling
Debounce windows, quarantine triggers, alert emission.


Phase 5: Automation dispatch
End‑to‑end flow
Readiness → queue → run metadata capture.



TDD sequencing keeps ingestion behavior predictable: write tests for readiness and hashing first, implement minimal logic to satisfy them, then expand into watcher and dispatch integration while preserving audit logs and receipt integrity.

text: Automation mode is now designed to be activated by either a CLI flag (--automation) or a task-config key (automation_mode) embedded in Python task modules. title: Executed Document: RFC 001 - Introduction to AutoCleanEEG Pipeline
text:
This document executes the instruction to write an introduction to the big picture of what AutoCleanEEG Pipeline is.



Based on the codebase exploration, AutoCleanEEG Pipeline is a modular framework for automated EEG data processing. Key components include:

Core pipeline orchestration
Modular processing functions (preprocessing, ICA, epoching, artifacts)
Plugin system for file formats
CLI interface
Task configuration system
BIDS support
Built-in tasks for various paradigms




AutoCleanEEG Pipeline is a comprehensive, automated framework for EEG data preprocessing that streamlines the complex process of cleaning and preparing electroencephalography (EEG) data for analysis. Built on the robust MNE-Python library, it offers a modular “lego block” approach that allows users to construct customized preprocessing pipelines tailored to their specific experimental paradigms and data characteristics.
The pipeline supports a wide range of EEG paradigms including Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR), Mismatch Negativity (MMN), resting state, and more, making it versatile for both research and clinical applications. Its design emphasizes research workflows, BIDS compatibility for standardized data organization, and detailed quality control outputs to ensure data integrity.



Modular Architecture: Processing steps are provided as interchangeable blocks, allowing flexible pipeline construction without coding.
Automated Quality Assurance: Built-in artifact detection, channel rejection, and epoch quality flagging with statistical methods.
BIDS Compliance: Standard data organization and metadata handling for reproducible research.
Extensible System: Plugin architecture for custom file formats and processing steps.
Batch Processing: Efficient handling of multiple files with parallel execution and database logging.
Comprehensive Reporting: PDF reports, visualizations, and metadata summaries for transparency.
Task System: Pre-configured tasks for common paradigms with customizable parameters.




The pipeline is designed for neuroscientists, clinicians, and data analysts who need reliable, reproducible EEG preprocessing. It serves:

Researchers: Automate routine preprocessing to focus on scientific questions
Clinicians: Standardize processing for consistent clinical EEG analysis

Developers: Extensible framework for custom EEG processing tools




AutoCleanEEG fits into the EEG processing workflow as the preprocessing stage, taking raw EEG data and producing clean, analysis-ready datasets. It bridges the gap between data acquisition and statistical analysis, ensuring data quality while reducing manual processing time.
By automating routine cleaning tasks, it allows researchers to focus on their scientific questions while maintaining high standards of data quality and processing transparency.




This introduction is saved as a dedicated page in the plans website and linked in the navigation.

AutoCleanEEG Pipeline is a comprehensive, automated framework for EEG data preprocessing that streamlines the complex process of cleaning and preparing electroencephalography (EEG) data for analysis. Built on the robust MNE-Python library, it offers a modular “lego block” approach that allows users to construct customized preprocessing pipelines tailored to their specific experimental paradigms and data characteristics.
The pipeline supports a wide range of EEG paradigms including Auditory Steady-State Response (ASSR), Mismatch Negativity (MMN), resting state, and more, making it versatile for both research and clinical applications. Its design emphasizes research workflows, BIDS compatibility for standardized data organization, and detailed quality control outputs to ensure data integrity.



Modular Architecture: Processing steps are provided as interchangeable blocks, allowing flexible pipeline construction without coding.
Automated Quality Assurance: Built-in artifact detection, channel rejection, and epoch quality flagging with statistical methods.
BIDS Compliance: Standard data organization and metadata handling for reproducible research.
Extensible System: Plugin architecture for custom file formats and processing steps.
Batch Processing: Efficient handling of multiple files with parallel execution and database logging.
Comprehensive Reporting: PDF reports, visualizations, and metadata summaries for transparency.
Task System: Pre-configured tasks for common paradigms with customizable parameters.




The pipeline is designed for neuroscientists, clinicians, and data analysts who need reliable, reproducible EEG preprocessing. It serves:

Researchers: Automate routine preprocessing to focus on scientific questions
Clinicians: Standardize processing for consistent clinical EEG analysis

Developers: Extensible framework for custom EEG processing tools




AutoCleanEEG fits into the EEG processing workflow as the preprocessing stage, taking raw EEG data and producing clean, analysis-ready datasets. It bridges the gap between data acquisition and statistical analysis, ensuring data quality while reducing manual processing time.
By automating routine cleaning tasks, it allows researchers to focus on their scientific questions while maintaining high standards of data quality and processing transparency.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text: Automation requires repeatable runs that reuse a stable output root, yet the current pipeline backs up existing task directories on the first encounter per process. The refined autocleaneeg-pipeline serve model introduces a dedicated automation workspace with test/live runtime isolation, operator-facing YAMLs, hidden deployed configs, and event-driven ingestion using Python watchfiles backed by Rust notify. This revision strengthens the idempotency plan by specifying workspace governance, config promotion, file-watching safety gates, and output policies that preserve uptime, auditability, and reproducibility.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Operating Requirements
The automation manager must support high uptime, safe configuration promotion, and deterministic workspace management while preserving the existing audit trail. The requirements below constrain the design and inform the idempotency strategy.

Table 1. Operational requirements for serve-mode automation.







Requirement
Rationale
Implication




Uptime-safe config promotion
Operators edit YAMLs directly
Promote to hidden deployed configs with atomic swaps.


Runtime isolation
Test changes cannot touch live runs
Maintain runtimes/test and runtimes/live.


Idempotent outputs
Repeated runs must reuse folders
Adopt run-scoped naming and overwrite policy.


Ingestion readiness
Avoid partial file ingestion
Use watchfiles + notify with stability windows.


Auditability
Trace config and runtime changes
Append-only metadata and deployment logs.


Workspace determinism
Taskfile + montage define automation
Enforce taskfile-montage-version naming.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Current Backup Mechanism
The backup trigger lives in step_prepare_directories, where an existing task root is moved to a timestamped backup directory before new BIDS-compliant subdirectories are created. The behavior is invoked by Pipeline during every run, and any backup event is captured in the database metadata as directory_backup, then used by resolve_moved_path in src/autoclean/utils/path_resolution.py to repair legacy paths. The net effect is that every new CLI invocation generates a fresh output root, which is ideal for safety but unsuitable for automation workflows that must append artifacts to a single target.





flowchart LR
  A[Existing task root] --> B{First encounter
in process?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Move to task_backup_timestamp]
  B -->|No| D[Reuse task root]
  C --> D
  D --> E[Create/ensure BIDS, reports, exports, QA]


 Figure 1. Task-root backup flow during directory preparation.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Serve Workspace Architecture
The serve workflow introduces a distinct automation workspace that is self-contained and deliberately structured to maintain separation between test and live operations. Within this folder, runtimes/test and runtimes/live host isolated pipeline runtimes, while serve-test.yaml and serve-live.yaml live at the workspace root for operator edits. Each automation workspace under the parent folder is named using the taskfile-montage-version convention to make provenance explicit and to align with the stated requirement that a task file plus montage uniquely define an automation instance. A lightweight workspace registry should track the active serve root, enforce naming conventions, and prevent accidental mixing of test and live artifacts.





flowchart TD
  A[serve-workspace/] --> B[runtimes/]
  B --> C[test/]
  B --> D[live/]
  A --> E[serve-test.yaml]
  A --> F[serve-live.yaml]
  A --> G[deploy/validated-yaml]
  A --> H[taskfile-montage-version/]


 Figure 2. Proposed autocleaneeg-serve workspace layout. 




Table 2. Serve workspace components and responsibilities.







Component
Purpose
Notes




runtimes/test
Isolated test runtime installation
Enables safe validation without disrupting live runs.


runtimes/live
Production runtime installation
Serves active workloads with pinned versions.


serve-test.yaml
Operator-facing test configuration
Edited directly; validated before deployment.


serve-live.yaml
Operator-facing live configuration
Edited directly; validated before deployment.


deploy/
Hidden deployed YAMLs
Replaced only after validation passes.


taskfile-montage-version/
Automation workspace
Contains per-automation task outputs and logs.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Runtime Management and Versioning
The serve workspace isolates runtime installs to preserve reproducibility and allow safe upgrades. The test runtime is the proving ground for new versions and configuration changes, while the live runtime stays pinned to the deployed YAML until a validated promotion occurs.

Table 3. Runtime management responsibilities in the serve workspace.








Action
Test Runtime
Live Runtime
Notes




Install
Allow new builds
Not touched
Track semantic version and build metadata.


Upgrade
Validate with test config
Promote after deploy
Require rollback plan.


Rollback
Reset to prior build
Restore last known good
Keep archived runtimes.


Health check
Run validation suite
Monitor uptime
Log to audit records.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Command Family and Governance
The autocleaneeg-pipeline serve command family acts as the automation manager. It must accept either an existing serve workspace path or create a new one, then provide a consistent set of control verbs so operators can manage configuration, validation, and deployment without manual file shuffling.

Table 4. Serve command family expectations.







Command
Purpose
Expected Behavior




serve workspace
Set or edit serve workspace
Creates or updates the active automation workspace pointer.


serve list
Enumerate automations
Lists test/live configurations and workspace status.


serve validate
Dry-run config validation
Runs against test or live config without deployment.


serve deploy
Promote validated config
Replaces hidden deployed YAML and activates runtime.









NoteConfiguration Safety



Live uptime requires that serve-test.yaml and serve-live.yaml are never used directly by automation. The system should validate these files, then atomically replace hidden deployed YAMLs in the deploy/ path to avoid partial or invalid updates.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Workspace Lifecycle and Deployment Workflow
The serve workspace must support a predictable lifecycle that separates operator edits, validation, and deployment while keeping the runtime isolation intact. The workflow below formalizes how the automation manager should create or attach to a workspace, validate YAML updates, and promote them into the hidden deployed set used by the automation engine.





flowchart TD
  A["Select or create serve workspace"] --> B["Initialize runtimes test/live"]
  B --> C["Edit serve-test.yaml or serve-live.yaml"]
  C --> D["serve validate dry-run"]
  D -->|Pass| E["Promote to deploy hidden YAML"]
  D -->|Fail| F["Reject and report errors"]
  E --> G["serve deploy activates runtime"]


 Figure 3. Serve workspace lifecycle and deployment flow.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Ingestion Monitoring and Watch Strategy
Automation should avoid blind polling of ingestion folders. A hybrid event-driven approach using Python watchfiles with the Rust notify backend provides low-latency file events while allowing deterministic readiness checks before a run is dispatched. The ingestion system should debounce file events, verify size stability, and optionally require a sentinel file (e.g., .ready) before a dataset is queued.





flowchart LR
  A[watchfiles + notify events] --> B[debounce window]
  B --> C[readiness checks]
  C -->|Pass| D[queue automation run]
  C -->|Fail| E[quarantine + retry]
  D --> F[dispatch pipeline runtime]


 Figure 4. Event-driven ingestion and run dispatch sequence. 




Table 5. Ingestion readiness checks for watch-based automation.







Check
Signal
Action




Stability window
File size unchanged for N seconds
Mark dataset ready for validation.


Sentinel file
.ready marker or manifest present
Allow immediate queueing.


Extension filter
Only accept configured extensions
Ignore partial or hidden files.


Quarantine rule
Missing metadata or corrupt header
Move to quarantine folder and alert.


Retry policy
Transient IO errors
Backoff and re-check.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
YAML Configuration Intent
The serve YAML files encode runtime selection, ingestion boundaries, watch settings, and the taskfile/montage combinations used to derive automation workspace names. The intent is to minimize operator input while preserving rigorous controls over what the automation engine executes, including explicit readiness windows and ingestion guards. Operator-facing YAMLs must be validated and copied into hidden deployed configs before activation.

Table 6. Candidate YAML keys for serve automation.







Key
Purpose
Notes




mode
Test/live switch
Directs validation or deployment.


automation_mode
Backup bypass
Default automation flag when CLI absent.


runtime
Runtime path
Must point to runtimes/test or runtimes/live.


watch_backend
File watcher
Use notify via watchfiles.


settle_seconds
Stability window
Prevents partial ingestion.


ingestion_folders
Ingestion roots
Avoid incomplete staging areas.


ingestion_sentinel
Ready marker
Overrides stability window when present.


quarantine_dir
Quarantine root
Holds failed or incomplete datasets.


workspace_name
Naming template
Use taskfile-montage-version.


taskfile
Task definition
Combined with montage for workspace naming.


montage
Montage ID
Aligns with taskfile choice.


output_policy
Idempotency rule
Example run_id_suffix.



mode: live
automation_mode: true
runtime: runtimes/live
watch_backend: notify
settle_seconds: 30
ingestion_folders:
  - /data/inbox/live
  - /data/inbox/archive
ingestion_sentinel: ".ready"
quarantine_dir: quarantine
workspace_name: "taskfile-montage-version"
taskfile: RestingEyesOpen
montage: standard_1020
output_policy: run_id_suffix
The listing above illustrates the minimal schema elements implied by the user requirements, emphasizing runtime selection, ingestion boundaries, and the taskfile/montage pairing that drives workspace naming. Any implementation must ensure that the deployed YAML is versioned and that updates are atomic after validation.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Downstream Artifacts Affected
Disabling backups changes how several output families accumulate across runs. The core directories are created under the task root, and many downstream tools assume those paths are stable. The table below summarizes the primary artifacts affected if backups are skipped.

Table 8. Output artifacts affected by disabling task-root backups.







Artifact/Directory
Examples
Impact When Backups Are Disabled




bids/derivatives
Cleaned data, staged FIF/SET files
Files may be overwritten if naming is deterministic; may need run-scoped subfolders.


reports/
PDF QA reports, summaries
Reports accumulate; repeated run outputs may need versioning.


exports/
Final exported datasets
Overwrite risk if filenames repeat; automation should define overwrite policy.


ica/
ICA FIF caches, component notes
Cache reuse may be beneficial but needs collision awareness.


qa/
QA images and metrics
Re-runs can append; consider run identifier in filenames.


status/
run_id.json markers
Task-level markers can be overwritten; run-level markers remain additive.


pipeline.db
Run metadata, audit log
Single DB becomes authoritative; must remain append-only for compliance.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Automation Mode Precedence
Automation mode can be set either through a CLI flag (--automation) or a YAML key in the deployed serve configuration. To avoid ambiguity, the system must define precedence and record the resolved value in the run metadata.

Table 7. Automation mode precedence and audit rules.








Input
Scope
Precedence
Behavior




CLI --automation
Per-run
Highest
Overrides YAML for that invocation.


YAML automation_mode
Deployed config
Default
Applied when CLI flag is absent.


Runtime metadata
Per-run
Recorded
Logs resolved mode and source.









NotePrecedence Rule



If a CLI flag is provided, it supersedes the YAML key for that run. The resolved value is persisted in metadata to keep audit trails deterministic.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Idempotency and Output Policy
Automation mode disables the task-root backup, so idempotency must be enforced by output naming conventions and append-only metadata practices rather than directory rotation. The following policies keep repeated runs traceable while allowing the workspace to accumulate results.

Append a run_id suffix to reports, exports, and non-append files.
Keep pipeline.db append-only and record the active runtime, config hash, and validation status.
Preserve run-level status markers; avoid deleting previous run outputs unless explicitly archived.
Allow optional per-run subfolders for artifacts that cannot safely overwrite.







TipIdempotency Default



Default to a run_id suffix policy unless an automation explicitly opts into overwrite semantics.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Toggle Options and Automation Mode
A surgical toggle should avoid global behavior changes while enabling automation use cases. The most constrained options are (a) a CLI or API flag that disables the backup only for a single run, or (b) reusing the existing workspace.auto_backup configuration as a feature flag. The latter already defaults to True in src/autoclean/utils/config.py and is enforced during setup, so a new automation command could temporarily set it to False for an isolated run without altering user defaults.

Table 9. Candidate toggle mechanisms for automation mode.








Option
Scope
Pros
Risks




CLI flag --automation
Per-run
Minimal blast radius; explicit intent
Must be propagated through CLI → Pipeline → step_prepare_directories.


Config override workspace.auto_backup
Workspace
Aligns with existing config model
Needs guardrails to avoid accidental permanent disable.


Environment variable AUTOCLEAN_AUTOMATION=1
Session
Easy for automation scripts
Less discoverable; must be documented.









NoteRecommendation



Use a per-run automation flag that sets auto_backup=False only for that invocation, leaving the default safety posture intact. This supports the proposed autocleaneeg serve workflow without permanently altering workspace configuration.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
First-Step Plan

Finalize the serve workspace specification (layout, registry, naming conventions).
Implement the serve workspace and serve list commands to manage workspace selection and reporting.
Add serve validate and serve deploy to promote operator YAMLs into hidden deployed configs with atomic swaps.
Build the ingestion watcher using watchfiles + notify with debounce, sentinel, and quarantine policies.
Introduce the automation_mode toggle to bypass backups and enforce run-scoped output naming.
Extend run metadata to capture runtime version, config hash, and ingestion events for auditability.
Document overwrite policies and rollback procedures for test/live runtime promotion.

title: RFC 002: Automation Idempotency Preparation
text:
Discussion: Idempotency and Run Coexistence
Idempotency requires that a run can be repeated without corrupting or fragmenting outputs. Skipping the backup restores folder stability but raises overwrite risks for deterministic filenames. The safest mitigation is to append run_id or timestamp suffixes for files that are not inherently append-only, while leaving database and status logging as append-only records. Test/live separation and watch-based ingestion provide additional safety valves: validation runs exercise the exact runtime and config layout without touching production outputs, and readiness gates prevent incomplete data from entering live automation.

title: RFC 008: Ingestion Product Requirements Document
text:
Background and Context
Automation mode must safely ingest files without processing partial copies or duplicating runs. The pipeline already computes file hashes and maintains run metadata; the ingestion layer must formalize readiness gating, provenance receipts, and dispatch rules so automation can operate continuously without operator intervention. RFC 002 defines the serve workspace governance, and RFC 007 established per‑file readiness with hashing as the default. This PRD translates those decisions into implementable requirements and measurable outcomes.

title: RFC 008: Ingestion Product Requirements Document
text:
Provenance Model and Receipts
A deterministic ingestion layout requires stable subfolders. The recommended approach hashes the relative ingest path + minimal metadata (site, subject, session, acquisition date, batch ID) so the same dataset maps to the same folder across machines. Each folder contains a JSON receipt (same basename as the folder) capturing hash inputs, file list, file hashes, timestamps, and validation status, with revisions appended on updates rather than overwriting prior entries.

Table 5. JSON receipt schema (high‑level).


Receipt Field
Description




receipt_version
Schema version for backward compatibility


hash_inputs
Relative path + metadata used in hash


hash_value
Deterministic folder hash


files
File list with per‑file hashes and sizes


timestamps
Copy, validation, and update times


status
Ready, pending, quarantined, or deployed


revisions
Append‑only history of changes

Appendix A: Consultant Q&A Summary

Table 8. Consultant responses retained for implementation.






Question
Answer




Batch manifest tooling
Use upstream export/acquisition manifests with checksums.


Incremental updates
New run by default; allow short amendment window.


Pending → quarantine
24–72 hours pending; quarantine after 7–14 days.


Duplicate hashes
Skip by default; review only when compliance requires it.


Hash inputs
batch_id, subject_id, session_id, recording_id, site_id, device_id, export_time, timezone, file_count, total_bytes, manifest_checksum, operator.


Receipt retention
2–7 years per IRB/clinical policy.

title: RFC 016: Ingestion Loop Phase
text: This phase introduces a bounded ingestion loop that cycles through configured ingestion roots, dispatching ready files and stopping when idle. The loop uses the existing readiness and dispatch helpers, providing a safe, testable scheduler without a long‑running daemon.
